Codec

SBC, AAC

Water/dust resistance

IPX4

The Beats 360 are, first and foremost, fun headphones. That may not sound like much, but it’s a rarity in the sea of same-y over-ear headphones I’ve reviewed. The 360 have a slim, smooth design that’s appealing, with a soft-touch finish and an adjustable headband with smooth, telescoping metal (similar to AirPods Max or Sonos Ace Ultra).

The main draw of the 360s is the swappable headband and ear cups. With a slight downward pull, the headband comes off, and the ear cups do the same with a satisfying twist. In the box, you get a cushion set (headband and two ear cups) color-matched to the headphones, but mixing and matching colors is a big part of the 360's appeal (and its marketing).

Making them easy to remove also makes them easier to clean and replace—a headache with most other headphones—and I consider that crucial for anything I’m going to exercise with.

The cushions come in two fabric options: Performance Knit, a mesh-like fabric that’s decently breathable and durable, and UltraPlush, a much softer, faux-leather style material akin to what you’d find on other premium over-ear cans from Bose, Sony, and Sonos.

The Performance Knit ear cups are better for working out—they feel more breathable, especially when I start to sweat. For everyday listening, though, the UltraPlush is much softer and more comfortable over time.

To be clear, the Beats 360 didn’t make me suddenly love working out with over-ear headphones. I still think wireless workout earbuds, like Beats’ own Powerbeats Pro 2, are the way to go, but the 360s are absolutely better than other over-ear options. The clamping force is strong enough that the headphones stay secure for most (but not all) exercises, without feeling so strong that they’re uncomfortable. Bicycle kicks and sprints still caused them to shift around a bit, unsurprisingly.

On the scale, the 360 are a middleweight. They are heavier than Sony and Bose over-ear headphones, but lighter than the AirPods Max. It's a good balance. Could they be a little lighter? Sure. Do they feel super heavy? Not really.

I appreciate the physical button controls, especially when working out. I do wish the buttons were a little more distinct and easy to recognize by feel alone. Things like a small tactile dot on the volume up button or a slight divot between the volume up and down would go a long way to helping me distinguish the all-smooth buttons.

I found myself swapping to the UltraPlush cushions whenever I wasn’t working out, and I started calling this “normal mode” and the Performance Knit setup “sport mode." In everyday use, the slightly strong clamping force of the 360s switches from a pro to a con—they get uncomfortable to wear after a few hours of office work.

Noise-canceling and transparency are highlights here. While not as strong as flagship headphones from Sony or Bose, the Beats 360 are close enough, and the ANC plus natural sound isolation did a good job shushing coworkers, cafés, the office cafeteria, and crowded New York City subway cars. With ANC enabled, you get 32 hours of battery life, which is very strong.

Connectivity is also simple and easy. Like other recent Beats headphones, the 360s pair instantly with Apple devices, and they support Apple device swapping, Apple Find My, and Siri. On Android, you get fast pairing, Google’s Find Hub, voice assistant with a button press, a few other Google/Android audio switching features, and the stand-alone Beats app. There's no wired connectivity, which is fine, since a cord is the last thing you want to deal with while exercising.

It’s only when I listen to my favorite playlist in the comfort of my office that the 360s' biggest weakness reared its ugly head: sound quality. Simply put: They sound OK, but not for headphones that cost $350. Unfortunately, they do not sound nearly as good as the $300 Sony WH-1000XM4C, $350 Sonos Ace, or $370 Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen).

The first time I listened to music with the Beats 360 (after testing the Bose QC for weeks), I literally yelled, “Where are the mids?!” Listening on the Beats 360 feels like someone scooped out the midrange—guitars and vocals in certain genres seem weak or lost. On cheaper headphones, this wouldn’t be something I would harp on much, but for a $350 flagship headphone, it’s a miss, especially when the 360s get so much else right. Simply put, I won’t be reaching for the Beats 360 when I want to get lost in my favorite album or soundtrack.

Reliable Workout Buddy

I can see the Beats 360 doing very well for the gym. At $350, they're pricey but significantly less expensive than Apple AirPods Max, making them a good alternative for Apple users. To be fair, the Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen) and Sony WH-1000XM6 are also cheaper than AirPods Max and provide better sound quality than the 360s, but lack the fitness chops. The removable ear cups and headband are downright fun, and mixing and matching colors is a breath of fresh air in headphone land.

These are not the best-sounding over-ear headphones out there. They aren’t best in class at any one metric, actually. But the 360 are an intentional trade-off—OK everyday performance for superior workout performance. If that compromise is where the Beats 360 want to hang their hat, they’ve got next to no over-ear headphones putting up a good fight in the workout space.

Personally, I almost always wear wireless earbuds or open earbuds when I work out. I still find them vastly more comfortable and more convenient for the job. But that’s just me. And if the Beats 360 finally get people to stop wearing AirPods Max to run in, I’m rooting for them.

Harry Rabinowitz is a commerce editor at WIRED, where he covers headphones, earbuds, speakers, TVs, and fitness tech. Previously, he was the tech reporter at NBC Select, leading coverage and reviews of the same topics. Before that, he was a freelance writer for publications like Popular Science and Popular Mechanics. ... Read More

entries.title: Plastic Is Melting Onto Corals
entries.summary: Scientists have found a new form of pollution, one where plastic and pieces of coral become irreversibly intertwined.
entries.content:
Marine plastic pollution is rampant. That’s nothing new. Plastic waste has been found in a variety of marine ecosystems, including beaches, coral reefs, and even some of the ocean’s farthest depths. While a precise measurement is difficult, it’s estimated that several million metric tons of plastic lie on the seafloor.

Scientists have been recording marine animals entangled in or consuming plastic debris for over half a century, some even proposing the term “Plastocene” (the Plastic Age) to denote the geological epoch spanning from the 1950s onward. And now researchers have discovered a new way these substances are polluting the environment: Plastic is fusing with corals.

The discovery of this conglomerate—which researchers have dubbed “plasticoral”—was made during a survey of the beaches of the Ryukyu Islands in southern Japan. The scientists noticed small, brightly colored spots embedded in the white coral gravel. They collected samples from three beaches on the main island, Okinawa, and brought them to the lab where spectroscopic analysis revealed there were polymers derived from common household plastics.

Using micro-CT scans, the researchers determined that the polymers had melted into the microscopic pores in the fragments of coral skeleton, becoming so integrated that the two could no longer be separated.

This is also not the first time plastic has been found enmeshed with the natural world, though this phenomenon usually involves nonliving things like rocks. In 2019, another group of researchers found a thin layer of degraded plastic coating mussels and large algae in tide pools, which they called “plastiskin,” but this new study marks the first time plastic has been seen fused with corals.

And while coral rubble is no longer itself a living organism, even after being washed ashore, it often returns to sea later and plays an important role in coral reef ecosystems. It forms a stable foundation for new corals to settle on, and the irregular shapes make essential hiding places for small marine organisms to protect themselves from strong currents and predators.

How exactly the plasticorals may impact their living bretheren is unknown, though previous research has shown that some chemicals that can leach from common plastics inhibit coral reproduction. Other studies have found that plastic fragments can carry pathogens to corals.

Scientists are also not yet certain how the plastic is fusing with the corals. Though the temperatures of our oceans are ever increasing, they’re not quite hot enough yet to melt plastic. Ultraviolet radiation can also contribute, but the researchers consider beach bonfires to be the leading candidate.

Further investigation is needed to confirm this, but given plastic’s pervasiveness as a pollutant, it’s not unlikely that fires in even seemingly pristine areas are creating unintended fusions.

This story originally appeared in WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

entries.title: 19 Best Gifts for Plant Lovers and Gardeners (2026)
entries.summary: From smart apps and planters to unique tools, these gifts will turn even a black thumb into a next-level plant parent.
entries.content:
Ostensibly, plant lovers and gardeners should be the easiest people to shop for. Just get them a plant, right?

Wrong. (Well, most of the time.) I review indoor hydroponic gardens for WIRED and have been a proud plant parent for almost 30 years, so I can say that even if you have a running mental catalog of all your recipients’ plants and know which ones they don’t yet have, you may not know what they have space for, or what they’re looking to switch up to this gardening season.

In general, the best gifts are ones that work with the plants and garden they already have, or that help them care for them. I’ve dug through the dirt to vet, research, and real-world test gifts that will earn their keep, whether your recipient has a single cactus on a windowsill or a multi-acre farm.

For more gift ideas, check out our other gift guides, including Gifts for Bird Lovers, Gifts for Coworkers, Gifts for Book Lovers, and the Best Flower Delivery Services.

Updated September 2026: I’ve added a self-watering planter and a self-watering raised garden bed, gift boxes from Happy Happy Houseplant, monstera deliciosa candy, water-storing crystals, and an all-purpose garden tool. I’ve also ensured up-to-date links and prices.

Plants as Art

It’s difficult to overstate just how cool this 32" x 5" x 11" metal grow-light frame looks in person, which was inspired by shadowbox planters the creator saw in Paris. It not only adds a sleek, contemporary vibe to just about any home decor style, but it also isn’t as bright as a traditional grow light, so it’s not disruptive to keep in your living space. You can set an on-and-off schedule and adjust the brightness in Modern Sprout’s app, or just turn it on and off manually with a switch on the 9-foot cord. The light can accommodate fruiting, flowering, or vegetative plants, such as herbs; I use it to display succulents (and a random N’Joy pothos cutting). Note that it weighs 8 pounds by itself, and the included mounting hardware does not have drywall anchors. You may want to grab some at the hardware store, as I did.

For Foolproof Planting

Sol Soils products are on the pricier side, but if you know a plant lover who has a black thumb—or who just appreciates the best of the best—this line of specialty houseplant potting mixes, additives, and amendments is among the best I’ve ever tried. The houseplant chunky mix ($13) looks like an odd jumble of coconut husk chips, bark, pumice, and other bits and bobs, but it has saved many an ailing seedling in my household from the brink of death. Especially when paired with the Repot Recovery ($13) repotting shock treatment and Monthly Myco Mycorrhizal Fungi Inoculant ($13), a beneficial fungus that will help roots better absorb nutrients. All Sol Soils products are available for purchase individually, but if you’re not sure what your giftee may want or need, the themed gifting bundles are a great place to start.

An Artful Watering Can

I’ve been looking to add a watering can to this guide for more than a year, but none of the ones I’ve tried made the cut. Until now. A good watering can should have a long spout for reaching plants on shelves or on longer tables, and water flow that’s neither too slow nor too fast. It should hold enough water for more than a couple of plants, but not be too heavy to carry around, and also look good enough to sit out on display. This handmade borosilicate glass model hits all these points. It holds 32 ounces of water and comes in five colors (shown is Lilac/Emerald), and the fluted top makes it easy to fill yet hard to spill. Note that it is fragile, however, so it’s probably best in a home without small children or boisterous pets.

Automate Your Plant Care

This might be one of the most useful houseplant tools I have ever used, outside of a watering can. Planta is an app that serves as a central clearinghouse for your houseplants and their care needs. With Planta’s Premium subscription, it will set fertilizing and watering schedules based on more than 30 parameters, including local weather data, and will even turn your phone into a light meter to help you find the best spot for that particular species. I’ve been using Planta Premium for almost a year (as anyone who’s been around me knows, as they’ve probably heard me talk about it), and these care schedules have resulted in tons of new growth on my existing plants.

The app also has a “Dr. Planta” diagnosis feature, where you can submit photos of plant problems to see what might be wrong and how you can fix it. Premium’s most recent update included a new Quick Add tool, which will immediately assess any new plant additions to your household, the size and type of pot they’re in, and the nearby light conditions, helping to dial in an even more customizable care schedule. (It’s not perfectly accurate, but surprisingly close.)

Cute Houseplant Care

Happy Happy Houseplant makes plant-parent chores fun again with these cheery starter kits featuring everything from fungus gnat insecticide to soil revitalizers and plant food. (Or you can buy them all for $205—a savings of $50 over buying them individually.) Once opened, each box folds out into a cootie-catcher-esque shape with printed information, a colorful bottle of solution, a glass dropper bottle, and a set of stickers. (Ostensibly to stick to the glass dropper bottle, but they don’t stick super well.) I love these boxes and have tried them all at this point—they all work as promised, but my personal MVPs are the Fungus Gnat Death Drops ($45) and the mycorrhizal fungi Root Boost ($33), which helps grow symbiotic fungi in your houseplants and comes in an ice cream-style tub instead of the box.

For Keeping Houseplant Leaves Clean and Healthy

Houseplants have a tendency to gather dust, especially on high shelves or in particularly dusty areas like near a litter box. This is bad news for plant health any time, but especially so during the winter months, when leaves need as much light as they can get. If your giftee has plants with lots of long, thin leaves, like a corn plant or ponytail palm, the Goha Leaf Sweep is an invaluable tool—it features little microfiber “socks” that fit over lockable plastic tongs, so you can clean both sides of the leaves at the same time. I also like to lock it in place and use one side at a time for plants with larger leaves, like monstera or philodendron. The “sock” covers really do act like a magnet for dust, can be rotated in order to use every bit of clean surface, and are fully machine-washable.

Houseplant Candy

Trendy monstera deliciosa houseplants are everywhere these days, but did you know they actually produce a fruit? It looks a bit like a cross between corn on the cob and a pineapple and actually tastes a lot like the latter. I’ve never tried it, as apparently they can take up to a year to ripen and rarely produce outside of their native tropical climates (I did find one available to ship, but it costs $65), but Happy Happy Houseplant makes a saltwater taffy from it, which might be the next best thing. It’s quite tart, but it makes a super-fun gift for plant lovers or lovers of unique candies.

Grow Your Own Indoor Salad

This little six-pod hydroponic garden from my guide to the Best Indoor Gardening Systems offers decent yields with minimal fuss—all functions can be controlled by pushing or holding a single embossed AeroGarden logo on the top. (Once for on or off, five seconds for changing the time of day the light comes on, etc.) If you know someone who’s hydroponic-curious but intimidated by apps, pH testing, and the thought of daunting maintenance, this system is regularly on sale for under $100 and comes in five colors, including red, black, white, green, and “mocha.” However, note that it does NOT come with its own seeds or sponges, so you’ll want to throw in some grow sponges so your giftee can plant their own seeds. Some online reviews note longevity concerns, but mine has been in continuous use for nearly a year with no issues yet.

Grow Your Own Mushrooms

You have probably seen other brands’ versions of this kit, but those are usually stored dehydrated and are only good for one fruiting, if you’re lucky. North Spore’s are shipped fresh, with an enclosed little squirt bottle for keeping moist (sorry), so they’ll be good for multiple fruitings. My pink oyster mushroom block had three of them before it dried out. Oyster mushrooms are typically the most beginner-friendly, and North Spore offers two different kinds—pink and blue, as well as trendy lion’s mane if your recipient is a more experienced mycologist.

Suppose your giftee loves growing mushrooms but has graduated to more challenging varieties. In that case, North Spore makes an automated monotub ($150) that can be paired with either substrate or the brand’s fruiting blocks. It keeps the growing environment with the proper airflow and humidity, and I’ve grown so many mushrooms in mine that I’ve turned into a Crazy Mushroom Lady, leaving bags on neighbors’ porches and chasing down acquaintances in the grocery store.

A Decorative Indoor Trellis and Plant Saucers

If your friend or loved one is supporting their vines or floppy potted plants with bendable moss poles or, worse, a jerry-rigged ladder made out of duct taped pencils (it was an emergency, OK?), treat them to one of these hand-finished, laser-cut plant supports. There are staked and modular versions (my favorite is the wonderful-smelling, extendable redwood Zella) as well as coasters, wall mounts, and saucers that water your plants from the bottom. I have tested many of them—including the classic versions—and all have added a dash of style while lending critical structure to floppy and vining plants. (Though note the extendable ones can’t support heavy stems, just light vines.) Can’t pick just one? Check out Treleaf’s collection of gift bundles.

A Garden Tool That Does It All

A Japanese hori hori knife is a classic gardening gift—it’s got a measurement-marked, 7.5-inch concave blade that serves as a trowel, with one serrated edge and one knife edge. If I’m just doing light work and weeding, it’s often the only tool I’ll take into the yard, as it can serve just about any purpose—digging, excavating, cutting, sawing. This hori hori is designed in my local Portland, Oregon, and is truly gift-quality with a pakkawood handle and leather sheath. (It also comes with a keychain knife sharpener.)

Succulents in the Mail

Lula’s Garden’s heart-shaped box is featured in our guide to the Best Flower Delivery Services, and since then, I have had multiple people recommend the brand to me. I have now tried it, and I have to agree—this is an excellent gift. It’s fun, stylish, and priced the same as or even less than transient flowers. Not everyone is inclined to take care of a houseplant, but succulents are super easy to care for, and the box they arrive in doubles as a planter. (Temporarily—it will grow mold over time, as I discovered.) All you have to do is unbox and use the included pipette to add a few squirts of water. The gardens are contemporary yet neutral enough to fit in with just about any decor. Just a heads up that unboxing the gardens that come with rocks (like the Bliss) may be a little messy, but the more premium gardens (like the Urban) don’t have any loose parts and come out of the box looking exactly as they do online.

For Making Compost Indoors

As seen in our guide to the Best Kitchen Composters, the Reencle Prime doesn’t fully make ready-to-use compost, but it comes the closest out of any of the major brands. It functions a lot like a heated trash can—just throw your kitchen scraps in, and microbes will break them down over time into a sort of loamy mixture. When the volume of the Prime reaches the fill line, the mixture can be scooped out and added at a 1:4 ratio with potting soil, then left to cure for three weeks. After this, it can be used for both outdoor and indoor plants. Not only will it free up space in your giftee’s trash can and cut down on dangerous greenhouse gas production, it will make their plants happy.

A Chic Self-Watering Planter

This self-watering planter is made out of Beauta’s nearly indestructible stone-look PolyRock. I wasn’t sure how it would look in person, but it’s actually quite modern and stylish. It’s shallow, so likely best for succulents or smaller, more decorative plants, but it holds an impressive amount of water and kept the beet greens I planted in it perfectly watered for nearly a month.

A Do-It-All Cart

Don’t torture yourself with an inefficient wheelbarrow! A garden cart might seem like an odd gift at first, but this is the all-category MVP of my yard and household. It not only carries mulch, plants, and yard tools, but it can also tote up to 600 pounds for the small version and 1,200 pounds for the large, which has allowed me to transport everything from giant pizza ovens to bags of smoker pellets. The cart’s got a quick-release dump latch on the front and pneumatic tires that handle mud and sand with no problem. I’ve tested other carts in the past, but this is the only one that has earned a permanent spot in my garage. If your giftee lives on a large plot of land or needs to transport a lot of pots or other supplies around their house, this will be an invaluable companion. Note that it will require some assembly, but it didn’t take more than an hour.

A Self-Watering Raised Bed

If you only remember Sharper Image from its mall stores in the ’90s and the clearance section at Ross and Marshalls, you may want to take another look—this is the second item from Sharperimage.com that I’ve tried recently and been impressed with. (The first, in case you were wondering, was a nifty rolling toolbox stool.) This cedar raised garden bed is a quick, tool-free assembly and does an impressive job of holding water—the little green flower pops up above the fill tube when it’s empty, and sits down when it’s full, so it’s easy to see at a glance whether the bed needs to be refilled. (Which is not often!) Because it’s 30 inches tall, it’s super easy to plant and harvest without bending over, and you won’t have to worry too much about weeds. That said, I’ve found it’s the perfect buffet height for deer, so you may need to add repellent or cover it with caging.

For Flawless Vacation Watering

Florev is not the only soil waterer on the market made from potassium polyacrylate (a superabsorbent polymer, sometimes referred to as an “agricultural hydrogel”), but it is the first I’ve seen that features 5-gram sachets that are easy to transport and/or gift. (One 4.4-ounce pack comes with 25 sticks.) This stuff really works, too—I added it to a potted pothos and the beads absorbed water to become a sort of gel, keeping the soil moisturized for the promised three weeks. It will hydrate and rehydrate over time as you water your plant, and will help cut down on overwatering by absorbing excess water. It makes a great gift for a plant lover who’s going on a long trip or struggling with under- or overwatering.

A Candle That Smells Like Tomatoes

You might be thinking: Why on earth would someone want a candle that smells like a tomato? I certainly did, when WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe crowned a tomato-scented candle as the overall best pick in her Guide to the Best Scented Candles. However, now that I’ve smelled it myself, along with a handful of other versions (LAFCO’s is my second favorite), I completely get it. I was immediately transported back to being amid sun-warmed tomato leaves in my grandfather’s garden, but my teen son, who doesn’t have the same association, also immediately recognized it as a distinctly summer smell. It’s warm and vegetal, but still sweet and fresh. It’s sure to remind your favorite gardener of the good times ahead.

A Quality Pair of Gloves

I’ve used a lot of gardening gloves over the years, but these two are my all-time favorites. Digz’s long-cuff garden gloves keep dirt, leaves, and other detritus out when you’re reaching down deep into something, and they’re invaluable for pulling out blackberry vines, goosegrass, and other long and/or sticky weeds. (Digz also makes some excellent tools with soft, ergonomic handles, but those aren’t as widely available.) If you’re looking for something sturdier, longer-lasting, and more versatile, Vermont Glove has been hand-sewing goat-leather gloves since 1920, and the Flatlander design dates from that time. These gloves are both ridiculously soft and insanely sturdy—my husband and I both used them all spring and summer for yard work, including pulling thorny weeds, and they have stood up beautifully despite their lightweight feel.

How to Fix a Motorola Coupon Code That’s Not Working

For those that require a coupon or Motorola promo code, enter it on the checkout page where it says “apply coupon.” But what if the coupon doesn’t work? First, review the product exclusions, expiration dates, and minimum order values. Some offers, like the military discount code, apply only to non-discounted phones.

Next, check that you aren’t stacking multiple Motorola promo codes. If you’re still encountering an error, make sure the code is entered correctly. Lastly, try clearing your browser’s cache or visit the site in an incognito window if the cart refuses to budge. Ultimately, the discount code may have expired.
